Jargon

JAR-gun -- two syllables, stress on the first syllable, JAR. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Jargon is the specialized vocabulary of a group, hard for outsiders to understand.

The skateboarders' jargon -- 'goofy,' 'ollie,' 'sketchy landing' -- left the new kid completely lost.

Worked Example

On her first hospital shift, the new nurse hears: 'Bed six is NPO pre-op, get vitals q4 and flag the attending stat.' She understands perhaps four of those words. By her third week, she is saying the same sentence herself without a flicker of thought -- and watching a visitor's face go blank at it.

The hospital's abbreviations are jargon: the specialized vocabulary of one profession. The worked example shows both of jargon's faces -- inside the group it is lightning-fast shorthand that saves lives and time; outside the group it is a locked door. That outsiders-shut-out effect is why the word usually carries a faint frown.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

shoptalk: Shoptalk is the relaxed spoken banter between coworkers about the job -- swapped over lunch, full of insider shorthand. Jargon is bigger and heavier: the whole specialized vocabulary of a field, written and spoken, the kind outsiders complain they cannot understand.

buzzword: A buzzword is a single fashionable term -- 'synergy,' 'disruptive' -- used more to sound current than to say something exact. Jargon is a field's entire working vocabulary, and however unfriendly it is to outsiders, it usually does real work inside the group.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

plain English: clear, everyday language anyone can follow

everyday speech: ordinary talk with no special vocabulary

Where it sits · how official the insider language is — lingo → jargon → terminology

lingo vs. jargon: Lingo is lighter and friendlier than jargon: casual slang worn for fun -- surfers' 'sets' and 'breaks' -- while jargon is the denser working vocabulary a whole profession actually runs on.

terminology vs. jargon: Terminology is more official than jargon: jargon grows up informally inside a group, but a field's terminology is its complete, settled system of exact names -- written down and taught the same way everywhere.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — jargon

root — jargon: the twittering of birds; meaningless chatter (Old French jargoun, probably imitative of bird sounds)

Put it together

Put it together: Jargon began in Old French as the word for the twittering of birds -- busy, chattering sound that carries no meaning to the listener. That is precisely how specialist talk strikes an outsider: rapid, confident, and incomprehensible. The word is probably imitative (built to sound like the chatter it names), and since echo-words leave no clean paper trail, its origin is marked uncertain.

Use the root in a new word: gibberish

Use the root in a new word: gibberish: The scrambled voicemail came out as pure gibberish.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Jargon is the insider vocabulary of a profession or group -- legal jargon, medical jargon, tech jargon -- and it usually carries a mild complaint: the word is chosen when the specialized language is shutting somebody out. Inside the group, jargon is genuinely useful shorthand; the criticism lands when it leaks into writing meant for everyone. Good writers translate jargon into plain English; careless ones hide behind it.
